analysis.one_liner: Expands Medicaid and CHIP to cover nearly all families, children, and single adults, regardless of income.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote, with no cosponsors, after being introduced in the final weeks of the 106th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every state to extend Medicaid or CHIP health coverage to families with children, covering incomes up to three times the poverty line, and to phase in coverage for single adults up to the same level by 2008. It would have made the Children's Health Insurance Program a permanent, open-ended entitlement instead of a capped annual fund, restored health coverage to lawfully residing immigrants, extended children's coverage through age 20, and let anyone above those income levels buy into the program at full cost. Employers would have had to tell workers without job-based coverage that they could buy this coverage.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured low- and middle-income families and single adults, who would gain access to Medicaid or CHIP coverage; lawfully residing immigrants cut off from Medicaid by the 1996 welfare law; young adults up to age 20; and homeless individuals reached by new outreach grants.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state to cover parents and children in families with incomes up to 200% of the poverty line in 2001, rising to 300% in later years, through Medicaid or CHIP, with enhanced federal matching funds [S2][S3].
Phases in Medicaid coverage for single adults with no other coverage, starting at 50% of the poverty line in 2003 and reaching 300% by 2008 [S2][S3].

Converts CHIP from a capped annual allotment to a permanent entitlement, appropriating 'such sums as may be necessary' each year, so eligible children could not be turned away for lack of funding [S2][S3].
Restores Medicaid and CHIP eligibility for lawfully residing immigrants that the 1996 welfare law had barred, and bars sponsors from being billed for the cost [S2][S3].
Extends children's Medicaid and CHIP coverage from age 19 to age 20 and adds vision, hearing, and dental services to required CHIP benefits [S2][S3].

Removes old welfare-related eligibility barriers, including the rule counting work hours (the '100 hour rule'), simplifies applications, lets schools hand out Medicaid and CHIP information with lunch applications, and automatically enrolls children who lose one program into the other [S2][S3].

Lets anyone above 300% of the poverty line buy into Medicaid or CHIP at the pooled average cost, with premiums that cannot be adjusted for health status, and requires employers to notify employees without job-based coverage of this option and forward their applications [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the expanded coverage and enhanced matching payments through an uncapped, permanent appropriation; and states, which would take on new coverage obligations and administrative work, though with higher federal matching rates. Employers would face new notice and payroll-withholding duties. Health plans selling individual coverage would face a government-run alternative for people who cannot find affordable private coverage.

drawbacks.text: The open-ended CHIP appropriation and expanded eligibility would substantially increase federal health spending, and the bill contains no financing mechanism or cost estimate beyond appropriations language [S2][S3].
States would be required to expand coverage and meet conditions regardless of their budget situation, though enhanced federal matching would offset part of the cost [S2][S3].

Offering public coverage to families above 300% of the poverty line and to single adults could lead some employers and workers to drop private coverage in favor of the public program, shifting costs to taxpayers [S3].
Employers of all sizes, including those with no health plan, would take on new administrative duties to distribute forms and withhold premiums from wages [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have come close to universal health coverage through the existing Medicaid and CHIP programs, reaching uninsured children, parents, and eventually single adults, at a large but unquantified federal cost. Its open-ended entitlement design would have guaranteed coverage but committed the Treasury without a financing plan, and its buy-in option risked pulling people out of private coverage. It was an ambitious expansion whose price tag was never scored or debated, because it never got past committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate's last working weeks of 2000, referred to the Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the BASIC Health Plan Act on October 5, 2000 [S1][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action was taken [S5].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a benefit, but the bill's potential costs never materialized: federal and state budgets were not expanded, and insurers and employers faced no new obligations or competition.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, insurers, and employers, spared new costs

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it at introduction; it was his only action before referral.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on October 5, 2000; no hearing, markup, or report was scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Set the agenda under which a last-session health expansion bill received no committee action or floor consideration.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, so no split can be measured; the bill had one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.industry: Health insurers (Medicaid and CHIP managed-care plans)
industries.note: Expanded Medicaid and CHIP enrollment would route millions of new members into state programs, which typically deliver care through contracted private managed-care plans, adding revenue for those plans. The bill also tightens conflict-of-interest and debarment rules on the vendors marketing that coverage [S2][S3].

The bill's buy-in option lets anyone above the income limits purchase Medicaid or CHIP coverage at pooled average cost, regardless of health status, giving uninsured people a government alternative to priced-out individual policies [S3].

Employers would bear new duties to notify uncovered workers and withhold premiums [S3]. But a public fallback for low-wage workers could also relieve pressure on employers who do not offer health benefits to add them.

States would take on mandatory new coverage obligations and enrollment work, but the bill sweetens the deal with enhanced federal Medicaid and CHIP matching rates and permanent open-ended CHIP funding [S2][S3].
